species.name: Inkcarp
species.description: A carp whose fins leave trails of ink in the water.
species.lore: Inkcarp write. Their ink trails form characters that scholars copy to practise calligraphy. Most of what they write is about waterfalls.

folklore_sources.tradition: The carp that strives to leap the Dragon Gate.

species.name: Scrollfin
species.description: A long carp with fins like unrolled scrolls covered in flowing script.
species.lore: Scrollfins gather below waterfalls and read aloud the characters their younger kin have written. Each one is sure it will leap the Gate next year.

folklore_sources.tradition: The carp that strives to leap the Dragon Gate.

species.name: Lantern Moth
species.description: A moth with papery wings that glow like a lit lantern.
species.lore: Lantern Moths gather at festivals and settle on unlit lanterns until they glow. Children count them for luck.

folklore_sources.tradition: Lantern festivals — the Lantern Festival in China, Hội An's lantern nights in Vietnam and Yi Peng in northern Thailand.

species.name: Lampwing
species.description: A great moth whose wingspan is patterned like a painted festival lantern.
species.lore: A Lampwing leads lost travellers home by flying just ahead of them. It never lands until they are safe.

folklore_sources.tradition: Lantern festivals — the Lantern Festival in China, Hội An's lantern nights in Vietnam and Yi Peng in northern Thailand.

species.name: Paddy Heron
species.description: A slender white heron that stands motionless in flooded rice fields.
species.lore: Farmers say a Paddy Heron in the field means a good planting. It can stand still from dawn until noon.

folklore_sources.tradition: Herons and egrets in ink painting as symbols of patience and purity.

species.name: Stiltsage
species.description: A tall, grey-plumed heron with a crest like a scholar's cap.
species.lore: Stiltsages are said to have read every scroll ever dropped in a river. They answer questions by tapping the water.

folklore_sources.tradition: Herons and egrets in ink painting as symbols of patience and purity.

species.name: Teacup Tortoise
species.description: A tiny tortoise whose shell looks exactly like a glazed teacup.
species.lore: Teahouses keep one on the counter for luck. Guests swear that tea poured beside it never goes cold.

folklore_sources.tradition: The tortoise as a symbol of longevity, and the tea ceremony's patience.

species.name: Teahouse Tortoise
species.description: A great tortoise carrying a miniature tiled pavilion on its shell.
species.lore: Small beasts shelter in the pavilion on its back. It walks one step an hour and has never been late for anything that mattered.

folklore_sources.tradition: The tortoise as a symbol of longevity, and the tea ceremony's patience.

species.name: Fox Ember
species.description: A slim red fox whose tail tip flickers like a candle flame.
species.lore: Travellers see lights bobbing along country roads at night and know a Fox Ember is out walking. Following the lights is a bad idea.

folklore_sources.tradition: Kitsunebi, the "fox-fires" — lights seen on country roads at night and blamed on foxes.

species.name: Pyrebrush
species.description: A fox with a great brush tail of living flame that never burns what it touches.
species.lore: A Pyrebrush leads processions of fox-fires along hillside paths on winter nights. It is not unfriendly, but it does enjoy watching people get lost.

folklore_sources.tradition: Kitsunebi, the "fox-fires" — lights seen on country roads at night and blamed on foxes.

species.name: Granary Mouse
species.description: A tiny brown mouse with a pouch of rice always tucked in its cheeks.
species.lore: A granary with mice is a granary with grain. Farmers count them, and grow uneasy when there are none.

folklore_sources.tradition: Mice and rats as signs of a full granary and household plenty.

species.name: Ricewarden
species.description: A plump, alert mouse that patrols granaries and drives off pests.
species.lore: A Ricewarden keeps exactly one grain in ten and guards the rest from everything else. Farmers think this is a fair price.

folklore_sources.tradition: Mice and rats as signs of a full granary and household plenty.

species.name: Mistkit
species.description: A small spotted cat with cloud-shaped markings that seem to drift.
species.lore: Mistkits are only ever glimpsed in fog. Hunters say that if you can see one clearly, it has decided to be seen.

folklore_sources.tradition: The clouded leopard of mountain forests, rarely seen and often said to be a spirit of the mist.

species.name: Cloudpelt
species.description: A long-tailed tree cat whose coat is a moving map of clouds.
species.lore: A Cloudpelt can climb down a tree head-first and hang by its hind paws. It watches villages from the canopy for years before it ever comes down.

folklore_sources.tradition: The clouded leopard of mountain forests, rarely seen and often said to be a spirit of the mist.

species.name: Callgecko
species.description: A spotted gecko whose loud two-note call echoes through the house at night.
species.lore: Families count a Callgecko's calls. An odd number means yes, an even number no, and seven in a row means a baby is on the way.

folklore_sources.tradition: The tokay gecko's call, counted aloud for luck or answers in households across the region.

species.name: Eavesgecko
species.description: A large gecko that clings to rafters and guards the household from pests.
species.lore: An Eavesgecko in the rafters keeps away insects, snakes and bad luck. Nobody evicts one; it would be like evicting a grandparent.

folklore_sources.tradition: The tokay gecko's call, counted aloud for luck or answers in households across the region.

species.name: Crag Kid
species.description: A small dark goat-antelope that bounds up cliffs on its first day.
species.lore: Crag Kids are born on ledges and learn to climb before they learn to walk on flat ground.

folklore_sources.tradition: The serow, a mountain goat-antelope of steep forests, admired for its surefootedness.

species.name: Cliffserow
species.description: A shaggy, maned goat-antelope with short spiked horns.
species.lore: A Cliffserow stands on one ledge its entire life. Climbers who reach it leave a pinch of salt, and it lets them pass.

folklore_sources.tradition: The serow, a mountain goat-antelope of steep forests, admired for its surefootedness.

species.name: Duskloris
species.description: A round-eyed loris that moves with dreamlike slowness.
species.lore: A Duskloris moves so slowly that people forget it is there. Its bite carries a sleepy venom, which it uses only when it has been very rudely treated.

folklore_sources.tradition: The slow loris, a shy night primate surrounded by many local beliefs about luck and misfortune.

species.name: Moonloris
species.description: A silver-masked loris whose huge eyes reflect moonlight.
species.lore: A Moonloris sees in the dark as others see at noon. It never hurries, and it has never once been caught unprepared.

folklore_sources.tradition: The slow loris, a shy night primate surrounded by many local beliefs about luck and misfortune.

species.name: Whistlepup
species.description: A rust-red pup that whistles instead of barking.
species.lore: Whistlepups are raised by the whole pack. A lost one whistles, and every adult within a valley answers.

folklore_sources.tradition: The dhole, a wild dog that hunts in packs and calls to its packmates with whistles.

species.name: Redwhistle
species.description: A lean red wild dog with a dark bushy tail and a piercing whistle.
species.lore: A pack of Redwhistles hunts in perfect silence, then whistles all at once. Keepers who bond with one often find the rest of the pack following them home.

folklore_sources.tradition: The dhole, a wild dog that hunts in packs and calls to its packmates with whistles.

species.name: Chirpling
species.description: A tiny green cricket with a surprisingly loud chirp.
species.lore: Chirplings sing on autumn evenings. Those who hear one on the first cool night say the summer heat has broken.

folklore_sources.tradition: Keeping singing crickets for their song, in carved gourds in China and small cages in Japan, as a sign of autumn.

species.name: Bellcricket
species.description: A bronze cricket whose song rings like a struck temple bell.
species.lore: Bellcrickets were once kept in carved gourds for their song. A kind Keeper set one free, and it followed her for the rest of her life, singing. They have chosen Keepers ever since.

folklore_sources.tradition: Keeping singing crickets for their song, in carved gourds in China and small cages in Japan, as a sign of autumn.

species.name: Hushhorn
species.description: A shy, chestnut calf with white face markings and two straight horn buds.
species.lore: Hushhorns are almost never seen. Forest folk say a Hushhorn only shows itself to someone who has stopped looking for it.

folklore_sources.tradition: The saola, a forest bovine of the Annamite Mountains, first described by scientists in 1992 and so rarely seen that it is called the "Asian unicorn".

species.name: Spindlehorn
species.description: A graceful forest bovine with long, straight, parallel horns that sweep back like spindles.
species.lore: A Spindlehorn walks so quietly that the forest does not notice it. Keepers who bond one say it is the patience of the forest given legs. It has never been caught, only befriended.

folklore_sources.tradition: The saola, a forest bovine of the Annamite Mountains, first described by scientists in 1992 and so rarely seen that it is called the "Asian unicorn".

species.name: Pebblepika
species.description: A tiny round-eared, tailless relative of the rabbit that whistles from the rocks.
species.lore: Pebblepikas whistle a warning when anything approaches. Mountain climbers learn the whistles and take them seriously.

folklore_sources.tradition: The pika of high mountain scree, which gathers piles of hay for the winter and calls across the rocks in sharp whistles.

species.name: Haymaker
species.description: A plump pika with cheeks full of flowers, standing guard beside a haystack taller than itself.
species.lore: A Haymaker spends all summer gathering flowers and grasses into a haystack under the rocks, enough to last the winter. Hungry travellers who find one and ask politely are given a handful; those who steal find the pass mysteriously full of whistling.

folklore_sources.tradition: The pika of high mountain scree, which gathers piles of hay for the winter and calls across the rocks in sharp whistles.

species.name: Highfoal
species.description: A long-eared, chestnut-and-white foal of the high plateau.
species.lore: Highfoals are born on the windiest plains in the Twelve Hours and can run within an hour of birth.

folklore_sources.tradition: The kiang, a wild ass of the high plateau, famous for galloping alongside travellers and racing them for the sheer joy of it.

species.name: Skyplain Kiang
species.description: A powerful wild ass with a dark stripe along its back, racing across the plateau.
species.lore: A Skyplain Kiang will gallop beside any traveller on the high plains, racing for the joy of it, then wheel away at the last moment. Nobody owns one. A few, very rarely, choose a Keeper.

folklore_sources.tradition: The kiang, a wild ass of the high plateau, famous for galloping alongside travellers and racing them for the sheer joy of it.

species.name: Tusklet
species.description: A smooth, grey piglet with two little tusks just beginning to curl.
species.lore: Tusklets gather at riverside salt licks with their families. Their squeals carry for miles at dawn.

folklore_sources.tradition: The babirusa ("pig-deer"), whose upper tusks grow up through the snout and curve back toward the forehead like antlers.

species.name: Antlertusk
species.description: A long-legged, hairless swine whose upper tusks curve up through its snout like antlers.
species.lore: Antlertusks grow their tusks through their own snouts and back toward their eyes, and they wear them with enormous dignity. Islanders say an Antlertusk's tusks keep growing until they point at the thing it most wants, and that it spends its life walking toward it.

folklore_sources.tradition: The babirusa ("pig-deer"), whose upper tusks grow up through the snout and curve back toward the forehead like antlers.

species.name: Gustferret
species.description: A slim grey weasel with tiny curved blades for claws, riding a whirl of dust.
species.lore: Gustferrets ride whirlwinds across mountain passes. Travellers with a strange shallow cut and no memory of how they got it have met one.

folklore_sources.tradition: The kamaitachi, sickle-clawed weasels riding the wind. In some regions they come as three; the first knocks you down, the second cuts, and the third heals the wound so it never bleeds.

species.name: Threefold Sickle
species.description: A silver weasel with sickle-blade forelimbs, always followed by two shimmering twins.
species.lore: Threefold Sickles hunt as one beast in three bodies: the first trips, the second cuts, and the third heals the cut before it can bleed. Keepers who bond one learn that it never means real harm. It just cannot resist a joke.

folklore_sources.tradition: The kamaitachi, sickle-clawed weasels riding the wind. In some regions they come as three; the first knocks you down, the second cuts, and the third heals the wound so it never bleeds.

species.name: Stormkit
species.description: A crackling blue-grey creature, half cat and half weasel, whose fur stands on end.

favoured_offerings: a dry place in a storm

species.lore: Stormkits fall with the lightning and are dazed for a day afterward. Farm children who find one in a field know to keep it dry.

folklore_sources.tradition: The raijū, a thunder beast that falls to earth with the lightning and was said to curl up in people's navels during storms, so children were told to sleep on their stomachs.

species.name: Thunderhide
species.description: A sleek beast of storm-blue fur crackling with lightning, its tail forked like a bolt.

favoured_offerings: a dry place in a storm

species.lore: A Thunderhide rides the leading edge of every storm in the Hour of the Dragon. When it grows tired it falls to earth in a lightning strike and curls up somewhere warm to sleep, which is why careful parents still tell their children to sleep on their stomachs during storms.

folklore_sources.tradition: The raijū, a thunder beast that falls to earth with the lightning and was said to curl up in people's navels during storms, so children were told to sleep on their stomachs.

species.name: Stubcoil
species.description: A short, stout snake with a fat middle and a stubby tail, like a little mallet.
species.lore: Stubcoils roll downhill when they're in a hurry. They are rarely in a hurry.

folklore_sources.tradition: The tsuchinoko, a stout snake with a body like a mallet, said to leap great distances and to like rice wine. Several towns have offered rewards for proof of one.

species.name: Hillmallet
species.description: A thick-bodied snake that can spring through the air like a thrown mallet.
species.lore: Towns in the Hour of the Snake have offered rewards for proof of a Hillmallet for a hundred years. None has ever been claimed. Hillmallets know about the rewards and find them very funny.

folklore_sources.tradition: The tsuchinoko, a stout snake with a body like a mallet, said to leap great distances and to like rice wine. Several towns have offered rewards for proof of one.

species.name: Emberstilt
species.description: A blue-and-red chick standing on a single long leg.
species.lore: Emberstilts appear where a fire is about to start. Villagers who see one check their stoves.

folklore_sources.tradition: The bifang of the Classic of Mountains and Seas, a crane-like bird with a single leg, blue feathers with red markings and a white beak, whose appearance was said to foretell fire.

species.name: Onefoot Pyrecrane
species.description: A tall one-legged crane of blue and crimson with a white beak and sparks in its feathers.
species.lore: A Onefoot Pyrecrane never causes the fires it foretells. It arrives first to warn, and those who heed it are spared. Those who ignore it say afterward that the bird must have started the blaze, and the Pyrecrane has long since stopped arguing.

folklore_sources.tradition: The bifang of the Classic of Mountains and Seas, a crane-like bird with a single leg, blue feathers with red markings and a white beak, whose appearance was said to foretell fire.

species.name: Drumcalf
species.description: A grey-blue, hornless calf that hops on a single sturdy leg.
species.lore: Drumcalves hop out of the sea before a storm. Their footfalls sound like distant drums.

folklore_sources.tradition: The kui of the Classic of Mountains and Seas, a hornless, one-legged ox-like beast of the Eastern Sea whose comings and goings bring wind and rain, which shines like the sun and moon and whose voice is like thunder.

species.name: Thunderdrum
species.description: A massive one-legged ox of storm-blue hide that glows like the moon, wind and rain swirling around it.
species.lore: When a Thunderdrum leaves the sea, the wind rises and the rain comes, and its bellow rolls across the water like thunder. An old story says a drum made from such a beast could be heard five hundred li away. Thunderdrums know the story, and they do not like drummers.

folklore_sources.tradition: The kui of the Classic of Mountains and Seas, a hornless, one-legged ox-like beast of the Eastern Sea whose comings and goings bring wind and rain, which shines like the sun and moon and whose voice is like thunder.

species.name: Sunnip
species.description: A black-and-red pup whose mouth glows like a coal.
species.lore: Sunnips leap at the sun at noon and yelp at how hot it is. They never learn.

folklore_sources.tradition: The bulgae, fire dogs from a land of darkness, sent to steal the sun and moon; the sun burns their mouths and the moon freezes them, so they bite and let go, causing eclipses.

species.name: Moonbiter
species.description: A large hound of fire and shadow with a scorched mouth and frost on its whiskers.
species.lore: Moonbiters were sent from a dark kingdom to steal the lights of the sky. The sun burned them; the moon froze them; they bit and let go, and that is why eclipses end. Those that gave up and stayed in the Twelve Hours make loyal, if moody, companions.

folklore_sources.tradition: The bulgae, fire dogs from a land of darkness, sent to steal the sun and moon; the sun burns their mouths and the moon freezes them, so they bite and let go, causing eclipses.

species.name: Reedstrider
species.description: A gangly creature with a horse's head and very long legs, hiding in the bamboo.
species.lore: Reedstriders lead lost children in circles until they laugh, then show them the way home. They cannot resist an audience.

folklore_sources.tradition: The tikbalang, a tall, long-limbed trickster with a horse's head who lives in bamboo groves and leads travellers astray; turning your shirt inside out breaks the spell, and three golden hairs from its mane are said to win its loyalty.

species.name: Balete Strider
species.description: A towering, long-limbed figure with a horse's head and a mane threaded with three golden hairs.
species.lore: A Balete Strider makes travellers walk in circles all night. Turn your shirt inside out and it laughs and lets you go. It will never bond with anyone who tries to pull its golden hairs, but it may offer them, freely, to someone who makes it laugh.

folklore_sources.tradition: The tikbalang, a tall, long-limbed trickster with a horse's head who lives in bamboo groves and leads travellers astray; turning your shirt inside out breaks the spell, and three golden hairs from its mane are said to win its loyalty.

species.name: Trunkcub
species.description: A golden lion cub with a short elephant's trunk and tiny tusks.
species.lore: Trunkcubs spray water at anyone who laughs at them. Everyone laughs at them.

folklore_sources.tradition: The gajasingha, one of the creatures of the mythical Himmaphan forest, with the body of a lion and the trunk and tusks of an elephant.

species.name: Tuskmane
species.description: A majestic golden lion with a flowing mane, an elephant's trunk and ivory tusks.
species.lore: Tuskmanes come from a hidden forest at the edge of the world, where creatures are made of two animals at once. One that leaves the forest brings the strength of the elephant and the courage of the lion, and it expects to be treated with the dignity of both.

folklore_sources.tradition: The gajasingha, one of the creatures of the mythical Himmaphan forest, with the body of a lion and the trunk and tusks of an elephant.

species.name: Duskmask
species.description: A small chimera with a monkey's face, a striped body and a hissing snake for a tail.
species.lore: Duskmasks call from rooftops at night with the voice of a mournful bird. Most people never see what makes the sound.

folklore_sources.tradition: The nue, a chimera with the face of a monkey, the body of a tanuki, the limbs of a tiger and a snake for a tail, whose eerie night cry was said to bring sickness until the warrior Minamoto no Yorimasa shot it from the palace roof.

species.name: Hollowcry
species.description: A shadowy chimera of monkey, tanuki, tiger and snake, wrapped in a black cloud.
species.lore: A Hollowcry rides a dark cloud over the palace roofs on sleepless nights, and its call sounds like a lonely bird. Legend says a great archer once shot one down. Hollowcries remember, and they are very polite to archers.

folklore_sources.tradition: The nue, a chimera with the face of a monkey, the body of a tanuki, the limbs of a tiger and a snake for a tail, whose eerie night cry was said to bring sickness until the warrior Minamoto no Yorimasa shot it from the palace roof.

species.name: Drumcub
species.description: A bright red-and-gold cub with a shaggy mane and a single small horn.
species.lore: Drumcubs dance whenever they hear a drum. Festivals start earlier when there is one around.

folklore_sources.tradition: The lân, a lion-like beast of good fortune whose dance, led by the jolly earth god Ông Địa with his fan, fills the streets at the Mid-Autumn Festival.

species.name: Moonlion
species.description: A magnificent red-and-gold lion with a single horn, a flowing mane and bells on its brow.
species.lore: At the Mid-Autumn Festival, Moonlions dance through the streets of the Twelve Hours, following a round-bellied figure with a fan. Children chase them, merchants feed them and the moon shines brighter wherever they pass.

folklore_sources.tradition: The lân, a lion-like beast of good fortune whose dance, led by the jolly earth god Ông Địa with his fan, fills the streets at the Mid-Autumn Festival.

species.name: Pestlebun
species.description: A small white rabbit with silver-tipped ears, carrying a tiny jade pestle.
species.lore: Pestlebuns appear only under a full moon, pounding dew into medicine on flat stones. By morning they are gone and the stones are clean.

folklore_sources.tradition: The rabbit in the moon pounding with a mortar and pestle, making the elixir of life in China and rice cakes (mochi, tteok) in Japan and Korea.
The Buddhist Śaśa Jātaka, in which a rabbit offers itself as food to a hungry traveller, who places its image on the moon in gratitude.

species.name: Jade Moonhare
species.description: A serene white hare with moonlight in its fur, standing beside a glowing jade mortar.
species.lore: They say the Rabbit was meant to run the Great Race but would not leave its mortar on the moon, and the Cat ran in its place. On the brightest nights a Jade Moonhare comes down to gather herbs, and those it finds sick wake well. It holds no Hour and wants none.

folklore_sources.tradition: The rabbit in the moon pounding with a mortar and pestle, making the elixir of life in China and rice cakes (mochi, tteok) in Japan and Korea.
The Buddhist Śaśa Jātaka, in which a rabbit offers itself as food to a hungry traveller, who places its image on the moon in gratitude.
